title: Adjectives and adverbs
subtitle: Position, order, comparison, gradable adjectives, and confusing pairs

rows.example: I love your **new** house.

rows.use: After verbs such as appear, be, become, feel, get, grow, look, seem, smell, sound, taste and turn
rows.example: The material this dress is made out of **feels rough**.

blocks.text: The verbs in the table above are not normally followed by adverbs. However, some of them can be followed by adverbs when the verb refers to an action.
blocks.note: She **looked angrily** at the man behind the counter.

items: After **as, how, so, this** (= so), **that** (= so) and **too**, adjectives come before the article.
I could never live in **as crowded a city** as Tokyo.
Tokyo's **so/that crowded a city** that I'd hate to live there.
I could never live in Tokyo — it's **too crowded a city**.

blocks.text: Some adjectives only appear after a verb and not before a noun. These include adjectives beginning with **a-**, such as **afraid, aghast, alike, alive, alone, asleep, awake**, etc.
blocks.note: A boy was **asleep** in the street. · There was an **asleep** boy in the street. (incorrect)

blocks.text: When more than one adjective is used before a noun, they usually appear in this order: **judgement, size, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose**. Sometimes they are separated by commas.

rows.example: We've got a **lovely little wooden** cabin in the mountains.
I love your **long, red, Chinese, silk** curtains.
What you need for your living room is a **large oak dining** table.

rows.use: To refer to members of a general social group
rows.example: We need to provide better housing for **the poor**.

rows.use: To refer to members of a specific group
rows.example: When the building collapsed, **the injured** were rushed to hospital.
**The French** have introduced new housing regulations in Paris.

blocks.text: There are three places in a clause where an adverb (or adverbial phrase) might appear: at the beginning, at the end and with the verb. Different kinds of adverb go in different positions, and some may go in more than one position.

rows.use: Adverbs do not normally appear between a verb and its direct object
rows.example: They built the house **very quickly**. (not *They built very quickly the house.*)

rows.use: With verbs formed using auxiliary verbs, the adverb normally follows the (first) auxiliary
rows.example: The town **has always been** popular with tourists. · Our house **will probably have been decorated** by the time you get there.

rows.use: Adverbs of frequency follow auxiliary verbs and **be** and come before other verbs
rows.example: I'm **rarely** in the city centre. · I **rarely go** to the city centre.

rows.use: Connecting adverbs usually go at the beginning of a clause
rows.example: We bought it as an investment; **then**, all the property prices in the area fell.

rows.use: Comparative: to compare things or people that are different
rows.example: Your flat is much **bigger** and **more comfortable** than ours.

rows.use: Superlative: to compare one member of a group of people or things with the whole group
rows.example: Mexico City is probably my **least favourite** city. · I think my home town is **the best** place in the world.
This area has become **considerably** more crowded and **far** noisier in the last ten years.
If you ask me, Ladybridge is **easily** the nicest area of town to live in.
Platinum is about **twice as expensive as** gold. · Iron isn't **nearly as hard as** diamond.
Iron isn't **nearly as** hard as diamond. · Gold is **not quite as** valuable as it was last month.

rows.use: nothing like as … as / nowhere near as … as
rows.example: Iron is **nothing like as / nowhere near as** hard as diamond.
The **taller** the building, **the greater** the fire risk.

blocks.text: **as** + adjective/adverb + **as** refers to a large difference between the things being referred to when used with **nothing like / nowhere near**. **not quite as** refers to a small difference.
blocks.note: Paper is **not nearly as** strong as plastic. · Gold is **not quite as** valuable as it was last month.

blocks.text: Ungradable adjectives describe qualities which are extreme and which cannot be 'more' or 'less', e.g. **amazing, dead, exhausted, fantastic, helpless, impossible, incredible, necessary, perfect, pointless, right, splendid, unacceptable, wonderful, wrong**, etc. Other adjectives are gradable.

items: With ungradable adjectives: **absolutely, completely, quite, totally, utterly**, etc.
With gradable adjectives: **a bit, a little, fairly, quite, really, too, very**, etc.

rows.example: After working on the building site all day, Tim was **absolutely exhausted**.
Pete was **a bit tired** after working on the building site all day, but it wasn't too bad.

blocks.text: When **quite** is used with gradable adjectives, it means 'rather, fairly'. When **quite** is used with ungradable adjectives, it means 'absolutely, completely'.
blocks.note: Our flat's **quite** nice, but not perfect. · I love your flat! The balconies are **quite** splendid!

blocks.text: Some words have the same form as an adjective and as an adverb and some also form adjectives with **-ly**. The different forms can have different meanings.

blocks.correct: Sandstone is not a **very hard** material. · Hit it **too hard** and you'll break it. · I could **hardly** hear the music.
blocks.incorrect: Hit it **too hardly** and you'll break it.

blocks.text: Some adjectives end in **-ly**, e.g. **costly, deadly, friendly, likely, lively, lonely, lovely**. They do not form adverbs, but we often use a phrase such as **in a … way** to describe how something is done.
blocks.note: She looked at me **in a very friendly way**.

exercises.title: A · Tick or rewrite
exercises.instruction: If the word in bold is correct, write a tick (✓). If it is incorrect, rewrite it correctly.

items.prompt: Whenever she gets home from work, Mum always seems **unhappily** about something.
I don't know what's in it, but it smells **strongly** of cinnamon.
When Terry finally became **calmly**, I asked him what had happened.
I'm glad I didn't go on holiday with Ely and Graham because it sounded **dreadfully**.
It's hard to believe that the seeds you planted have grown so **quickly**.
The car sped past me and turned **sharply** into the next street.
The actors could tell that the audience were growing **restlessly**.
Why are you looking so **accusingly** at me?
Add some chilli to the curry because it doesn't taste **spicily** enough.
I don't think I get **angrily** very often, but one or two people do really annoy me.
In the darkness, I felt **nervously** for the light switch and finally found it.
Tim appeared **tiredly** after his tennis match.

exercises.title: B · so / such / too / as
exercises.instruction: Complete the sentences using the words in bold. Add any other words you need.

items.prompt: I haven't had this ___ at work for a long time. (day, hard)
So ___ was it that I never went back to that country again. (experience, frightening)
If we'd known how ___ it was going to be, we wouldn't have agreed to do it. (difficult, task)
It was as ___ as I'd seen in a long time. (moving, performance)
Alex has got that ___ he never seems to have to work hard at school. (good, memory)
It was too ___ to turn down. (offer, tempting)
No matter how ___ you have, there's always the risk of failure. (career, successful)
I don't think I'll ever be as ___ as my brother. (good, pianist)

exercises.title: C · Adjective order
exercises.instruction: Complete the sentences using the words in bold in the correct order.

items.prompt: Oh, what a/an ___ sculpture! Did you buy it when you were there? (African, gorgeous, little)
Have you seen my ___ boots anywhere? I'm sure I left them here. (black, climbing, leather)
They've got some ___ shoes in the sale at Derbyshire's. (ballet, fantastic, pink, Russian, silk)
Didn't the bride look lovely in that ___ dress? (beautiful, cotton, cream, wedding)
Does Spencer still drive that ___ car of his? (blue, foreign, ugly)
It's hard to imagine that such a ___ frog is so important to the local environment. (Amazonian, green, tiny)
Andrea has a ___ rug on the floor in her bedroom. (long, lovely, sheepskin, white)
The clown was wearing a ___ wig and a red nose. (funny, plastic, red)
I couldn't believe it when Sylvia turned up in the same ___ hat that she wore last time. (horrible, wide, yellow)
When are you going to get rid of those ___ trousers? (dreadful, French, nylon, short)

exercises.title: D · Adverb position
exercises.instruction: Choose the best position for each adverb in bold.

items.prompt: The Millennium Dome, or the O2 as (A) it (B) is (C) called (D) now that the mobile company of that name owns the naming rights, has become a distinctive part of the London skyline. **correctly**
It was built for the millennium celebrations of 2000, and (A) a number of people (B) criticised (C) the high (D) cost of construction. **strongly**
Costing £789 million to build and operate for a year, (A) it (B) failed (C) to reach (D) its target of 12 million visitors. **completely**
Even Michael Heseltine, the politician who was originally in charge of the Dome, later admitted that (A) it (B) would (C) have been (D) better to build something else. **probably**
Although the press were critical, (A) people who visited the Dome (B) had (C) a positive experience (D). **often**
Even with low visitor numbers, (A) it (B) was (C) the most popular attraction in Britain in 2000 (D). **easily**
Although (A) it (B) is (C) closed (D), the Dome has a bright future as a venue for pop concerts and other events.
items.explanation: The implied adverb from the book is now/currently with closed: 'Although it is now closed' — position C.

exercises.title: G · Key word transformation
exercises.instruction: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first sentence, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between three and eight words, including the word given. Write only the missing part.

items.prompt:
The red shoes are slightly more expensive than the green ones.
**quite**
The green shoes ___ the red ones.
acceptedAnswers: are not quite as expensive as

items.prompt:
Richard is much more committed to the project than Grant seems to be.
**like**
Grant seems to be ___ to the project.
acceptedAnswers: nothing like as committed as Richard
nowhere near as committed as Richard

items.prompt:
If you argue about it more, we'll get to Denver later.
**the**
The ___ we'll get to Denver.
acceptedAnswers: more you argue about it, the later

items.prompt:
My new MP3 player was twice the price of yours.
**expensive**
Your MP3 player was ___ mine.

England is much bigger than Wales.
**nowhere**
Wales ___ England.
acceptedAnswers: is nowhere near as big as
is nowhere near as large as

items.prompt:

**nearly**
Annabelle ___ her brother, Derek.
acceptedAnswers: is not nearly as adventurous as

**the**
The ___ the crime rate.

**near**
